strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions are too coarse to specify contact regions, and the paper's part-level PAG representation with labeled part surfaces is a sensible, expressive solution.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is a clean, well-described coarse-to-fine constraint satisfaction pipeline (object-level pruning -> part-level alignment -> sampling/validation -> physics refinement) that gives a principled way to turn PAGs into physically valid scenes.

PARSE-10K is a substantial resource: 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets, 132 categories, dense contact annotations, and a part-level contact graph, which is a meaningfully richer annotation than prior datasets (Table 1 comparison is informative).

Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL on PARSE-10K yields large, consistent gains over strong commercial baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4) across three distinct spatial reasoning tasks, and the grounding-agnostic analysis helps disentangle localization from relational reasoning.

The scene-generation experiments show qualitatively richer, more complex scenes than a 3D-FRONT-trained baseline, and PAG conditioning is shown to matter via a user study with a clear preference pattern across complexity, realism, and contact fidelity.
weaknesses: The process for extracting PAGs from real images to seed PARSE-10K is only briefly mentioned ('extracting layout priors from real images') without methodological detail (automatic pipeline vs. human annotation, error rates, validation), making a key part of the dataset construction hard to assess or reproduce.

The conclusion admits PAG construction is 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses,' which raises concerns about the scalability, consistency, and potential annotation bias of the 10K-scene dataset that are not otherwise addressed in the main text.

The VLM evaluation trains and tests primarily on the same synthetic rendering distribution used to build the dataset; the real-image generalization check is described only as adding 'some manually labeled real images from COCO' without quantifying how many, or reporting results separately on this subset versus the synthetic test set, weakening the generalization claim.

No ablation studies are provided for the solver (e.g., contribution of coarse localization vs. part-level alignment vs. physics refinement) or for the VLM fine-tuning data composition (e.g., object-level-only vs. part-level supervision), making it hard to attribute the reported gains to specific design choices.

The scene generation comparison to InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT is confounded by differences in dataset scale/object density between 3D-FRONT and PARSE-10K, so the qualitative and user-study improvements may partly reflect dataset richness rather than the proposed method itself; no automatic quantitative metrics (e.g., collision rate, FID, physical stability score) are reported to complement the 20-person user study.

The comparison table (Table 2) does not include a baseline fine-tuned on the same data without part-level relations (only object-level), so the specific benefit of part-level supervision versus simply fine-tuning on more spatial data is not isolated.

Limited discussion of failure cases or scenarios where the directional-face contact model or DAG-based hierarchical assembly breaks down (e.g., cyclic/mutual support configurations, non-planar contacts), beyond a brief mention in the conclusion.

strengths: The core idea of part-level relational modeling (PAG) is a well-motivated extension of object-level scene graphs, addressing a genuine ambiguity in prepositional and object-level relations for scene synthesis.

The proposed two-level node structure (object/part) and the DAG-based hierarchical assembly formalism give a principled, tractable way to convert relational descriptions into geometric constraints and support efficient, largely rejection-free sampling.

PARSE-10K is a reasonably large dataset (10K scenes, about 50 objects per scene) with part segmentation and part-level contact graphs, a combination rarely available in existing indoor scene datasets (Table 1).
The paper demonstrates two distinct downstream applications (VLM fine-tuning and conditioned 3D scene generation), showing some versatility of the proposed data and representation.
Quantitative gains after fine-tuning (Table 2) and a user study favoring PAG-conditioned generation (Table 3) provide at least some empirical signal that the dataset and representation are useful.
weaknesses: The main VLM comparison (Table 2) pits a model explicitly fine-tuned on PARSE-10K against zero-shot general-purpose closed-source VLMs (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude) never exposed to this annotation schema or relation vocabulary; this is not an apples-to-apples comparison, and large margins likely reflect in-distribution fine-tuning advantage rather than demonstrated superiority in spatial reasoning. A fairer baseline, such as fine-tuning another model on a comparable non-PARSE spatial dataset or few-shot prompting with the relation vocabulary, is missing.

No ablation studies isolate which PAG components (object-level edges, part-level edges, DAG hierarchy, directional-face contact definition) actually drive the reported improvements, making it difficult to assess which design choices matter.

The scene-generation evaluation is thin: only a 20-participant user study over 12 scenes is reported, with no standard quantitative generation metrics such as FID/KID on renders, penetration or stability rates, or physical plausibility scores, despite the central claim of improved physical realism.

The Sec. 5.2 comparison confounds dataset and training pipeline: InstructScene is only evaluated as trained on 3D-FRONT and is never retrained on PARSE-10K, so reported gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the dataset or PAG representation versus the authors' own architecture changes (geometry encoder, FiLM conditioning, etc.).

The data-construction pipeline (extracting PAGs from real images, canonical pose assignment, part and surface labeling) is acknowledged as 'partially manual' in the limitations, but the manuscript gives no quantification of annotation effort, inter-annotator agreement, or failure rates, raising reproducibility and scalability concerns for a claimed 10K-scene dataset.

No direct quality assessment of the generated scenes themselves is reported (e.g., human judgment of realism or physical plausibility of PARSE-10K scenes in isolation, collision statistics, contact accuracy validation); all evidence for dataset quality is indirect, via downstream task performance.

The asset library covers only 132 object categories, which may constrain the diversity of real-world scenes that can be faithfully reproduced, and this limitation is not quantitatively discussed (e.g., coverage or failure rate when matching real-image layouts to available categories).

Key implementation and complexity details of the Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver (runtime, success/failure rates of constraint satisfaction, behavior on ambiguous part relations) are deferred to supplementary material not included here, limiting assessment of technical soundness and efficiency claims in the main text.

Several claims in the abstract and introduction (e.g., 'substantially improved physical realism,' 'significantly advances geometry-grounded spatial reasoning') are stated strongly but are only weakly supported by the limited empirical evidence (small-scale user study, in-distribution-only VLM comparisons).

strengths: The paper identifies and addresses a genuine limitation of prior spatial representations: linguistic prepositions and object-level scene graphs are shown concretely (via examples like 'book on table' or 'guitar leaning on bookcase') to be ambiguous about which specific regions are in contact, and the proposed Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) offers a principled, well-motivated fix by attaching relations to specific part/surface identifiers.

The DAG-based hierarchical assembly formulation is elegant: tying the acyclic property to unique-supporter physical relations gives a clean theoretical justification for tractable, sequential constraint solving, and the coarse-to-fine solver (object-level pruning -> part-level alignment -> sampling+validation+physics refinement) is clearly described and illustrated (Fig. 3).

PARSE-10K is a substantial, differentiated resource: 10,000 scenes, ~50 objects/scene on average, 132 categories, with part annotations and part-level contact graphs that, per Table 1, are not jointly available in existing datasets (HSSD, 3D-FRONT, FurniScene, METASCENES).

Empirical results are strong and consistent across two different downstream applications (VLM fine-tuning and controllable scene generation), suggesting the representation/dataset carries real signal rather than being useful for only one narrow task.

The fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model shows large, consistent gains over strong closed-source baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4) across three distinct evaluation formats (relation MCQ, part-contact MCQ, SGG), and the grounding-agnostic analysis helps disentangle grounding failure from relational reasoning failure, which is a thoughtful diagnostic addition.

The scene-generation user study shows a consistent preference pattern (PAG-conditioned > unconditioned > InstructScene/3D-FRONT baseline on all three criteria), supporting the claim that PAG priors help structure generation meaningfully rather than just adding noise.
weaknesses: The VLM comparison in Table 2 pits a model fine-tuned on in-distribution PARSE-10K-derived test data against zero-shot general-purpose baselines; this is an inherently favorable comparison for 'Ours' and doesn't isolate how much of the gain is from the part-aware representation itself versus simply from domain-matched fine-tuning. Fine-tuning at least one baseline (or reporting a same-recipe fine-tune on an object-level-only relation format) would better isolate the contribution of part-level supervision specifically.

The authors state in the limitations that PAG construction is 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses,' but the main text does not clearly describe how much manual effort is required per scene/asset, nor how this scales to the reported 10,000 scenes and 17,372 assets — this raises reproducibility and scalability concerns that are not adequately addressed in the body of the paper.

The scene generation quantitative evaluation relies solely on a small-scale user study (20 participants, 12 scenes), with a single baseline (InstructScene/3D-FRONT); no standard quantitative metrics (e.g., FID on renderings, physical-stability scores, collision rates, or scene-graph-conditioned generation benchmarks) are reported, limiting the strength of evidence for the generation claims.

No ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual solver components (e.g., object-level vs. part-level constraints, physics refinement step) or dataset design choices (e.g., effect of real-image layout priors vs. purely synthetic PAGs), making it hard to attribute the observed gains to specific design decisions rather than to the dataset scale alone.

The process for extracting PAGs/layout priors from real images is only briefly mentioned ('real-image layout priors') without methodological detail or quality/accuracy assessment in the main paper, which is a key claimed novelty (matching real spatial organization) but is under-specified for reproducibility.

The directional-face/near-parallel contact model is acknowledged to fail on oblique contacts, and no quantitative characterization of the frequency or severity of such failures within PARSE-10K is provided, leaving open how much of the dataset may contain imprecise contact annotations.

strengths: Introduces a novel part-centric relational representation (PAG) that meaningfully extends object-level scene graphs to part-level geometric constraints, addressing a well-motivated ambiguity (e.g., 'on' relations being underspecified at the object level).

Provides a substantial, well-documented dataset (PARSE-10K) with 10,000 scenes, part-level annotations, and part-level contact graphs, filling a genuine gap versus existing indoor scene datasets (Table 1 comparison is informative and the asset library construction pipeline, including part segmentation and semantic labeling, is described in useful detail).

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is technically clear, using a coarse-to-fine constraint-narrowing strategy (Algorithm 1) combined with physics simulation validation, which is a sound and reasonably efficient approach to avoid blind rejection sampling.

Demonstrates downstream utility on two distinct tasks: fine-tuning a large VLM (Qwen3-VL-235B) for spatial reasoning (with consistent, often large improvements over strong baselines like GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4) and improving a diffusion-based scene generation model with PAG conditioning, supported by both quantitative metrics and a user study.

Extensive supplementary material (dictionary of spatial relations, solver algorithm, dataset statistics, implementation details) supports reproducibility and gives confidence in the described pipeline's rigor.
weaknesses: The PAG construction itself is stated to be partially manual (200 hand-designed layouts inspired by real images, expanded to 10K scenes), which limits the scalability/automaticity of the pipeline and is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantitatively characterized (e.g., how much manual annotation effort per scene, or fidelity to source images).

The scene generation comparison (Sec 5.2) is only evaluated against a single baseline (InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT) and via a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes each); no quantitative generation metrics (e.g., FID, physical plausibility scores, collision rates) are reported, weakening the strength of the generation claims.

Scene Graph Generation results in Table 2 show fairly low absolute F1/precision/recall for all models including the fine-tuned one (76.6% F1 with bbox matching, but only ~41% Recall for competitors and even the fine-tuned model's numbers are relatively modest in the stricter with-bbox-matching setting), suggesting the task remains hard and the margin of improvement, while notable, should be contextualized rather than overstated as decisively closing the gap.

The categorization of only 132 object categories and asset retrieval-based instantiation (rather than free-form generation) may limit compositional diversity and realism compared to real-world scene diversity; this is not deeply analyzed.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual solver components (e.g., coarse localization vs. part-level alignment) or the specific effect of part-level contact graph supervision versus object-level supervision alone in the VLM fine-tuning experiments, making it harder to attribute gains precisely to the part-level innovation versus simply more/better data.

Comparison baselines for the VLM task are all fine-tuned differently (baselines are zero-shot/instruction-following pretrained models, while 'Ours' is fine-tuned on the paper's own training distribution), which is a natural but somewhat unfair comparison that could partly explain large margins; a more controlled ablation (e.g., fine-tuning Qwen3-VL on object-level-only data vs. PARSE-10K) would better isolate the value of part-level relations specifically.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually appealing part-centric scene graph representation (PAG) that fills a real gap between coarse linguistic/object-level relations and precise 3D geometric configurations, with a well-specified dictionary of part-level relations (Table 4) and clear motivation grounded in concrete examples (e.g., 'leaning against at its tip').

Provides a complete generation pipeline (coarse localization -> part-level alignment -> sampling/validation -> physics-based refinement) with an explicit algorithmic description in the appendix (Algorithm 1), which gives some transparency into how PAGs are instantiated into 3D layouts.

Produces a sizeable new resource, PARSE-10K, with part segmentation and part-level contact graphs, which is a type of annotation largely missing from existing indoor scene datasets (Table 1), and could be a useful resource for the community if released.

Demonstrates the representation on two distinct downstream tasks (VLM spatial reasoning fine-tuning and conditional 3D scene generation), showing consistent, nontrivial improvements over several baselines on both.
Reasonably thorough dataset statistics and appendix documentation (object/category distributions, contact counts, asset library construction, implementation hyperparameters).
weaknesses: The headline VLM comparison (Table 2) is not an apples-to-apples evaluation: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, and Qwen3-VL are evaluated zero-shot, while 'Ours' is the same Qwen3-VL backbone explicitly fine-tuned (LoRA) on PARSE-10K's own relation vocabulary, bounding-box format, and answer protocol. The large margins reported are expected simply from in-domain supervised fine-tuning and format matching, and do not isolate the contribution of the PAG representation itself versus generic benefit of training on matched-distribution data; no comparison with other models fine-tuned on the same data, or with PARSE's model evaluated zero-shot on external benchmarks, is provided.

The dataset's structural diversity is arguably overstated: the 10,000 scenes are generated from only 200 manually designed base PAGs (Appendix C.2), raising concerns about how much genuine compositional/relational diversity exists versus repeated instantiation/asset-swapping of a small number of hand-authored templates; this undermines claims of 'large-scale' diversity relative to datasets built from thousands of independently authored or scanned layouts.

No ablation isolating the effect of part-level versus object-level relations, or of individual solver stages (coarse localization vs. fine-grained alignment vs. simulation refinement), making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed part-level formulation specifically rather than engineering choices (asset retrieval heuristics, simulation cleanup, etc.).

The scene generation comparison in Sec. 5.2 is limited to a single baseline (InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT), which differs simultaneously in training data, object count, and task setup; this confounds the comparison and does not demonstrate improvement under matched conditions (e.g., InstructScene retrained on PARSE-10K, or PARSE evaluated on 3D-FRONT-style simpler layouts).

The user study (20 participants, 12 scenes each) is small, has no statistical significance analysis, and compares against only one competing method, limiting the strength of claims about realism/complexity/contact fidelity improvements.

No quantitative report of the solver's failure/rejection rate, generation time/cost for producing the 10K scenes, or sensitivity to asset/canonical-pose inconsistencies, despite the paper acknowledging in the conclusion that PAG construction is 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses' — this is a meaningful reproducibility/scalability concern that is not empirically characterized.

Significant portions of the core technical machinery (precise definitions of surface clipping, constraint region computation, solver subroutines) are deferred entirely to the supplementary algorithm, leaving the main paper's technical description somewhat qualitative and harder to assess/reproduce without the appendix.

The asset library and canonicalization process involve non-trivial manual verification and adjustment (Appendix B), which is a potential scalability bottleneck not discussed in the limitations beyond a brief mention, and makes it unclear how much manual effort underlies the reported 17,372-asset, 132-category library.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated representation, the Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG), that moves beyond coarse object-level scene graphs to explicit part-level geometric relations (contact surfaces, alignment, containment), addressing a real ambiguity in linguistic/object-level relational descriptions.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is a principled, well-engineered coarse-to-fine geometric constraint-satisfaction pipeline (object-level pruning -> part-level surface alignment -> collision-validated sampling -> physics-based refinement), and Algorithm 1 plus Table 4's relation dictionary give good technical transparency and reproducibility support.

PARSE-10K is a substantial, carefully constructed dataset (10K scenes, 17K+ part-segmented assets, 132 categories, 17 room types) with statistics (density, contacts per scene, part counts) that credibly demonstrate higher physical/relational complexity than existing datasets (Table 1 comparison is informative).

Strong and consistent empirical gains: fine-tuning Qwen3-VL on PARSE-10K yields large improvements over strong closed-source baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4) on visual relation MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, and scene graph generation, with a grounding-agnostic control analysis that helps isolate relational reasoning gains from grounding gains.

The scene-generation experiments (graph-transformer diffusion model conditioned on PAG) are supported by both qualitative comparisons against InstructScene/3D-FRONT and a human user study showing clear preference for PAG-conditioned outputs in complexity, realism, and contact fidelity.

Appendix is unusually thorough (asset library construction, contact detection pipeline via convex decomposition, dataset statistics, VLM fine-tuning prompts/hyperparameters, diffusion model architecture/training details), which substantially aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: PAG construction from real images is stated to be 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses' (acknowledged in the conclusion), and the paper does not clearly quantify how much manual curation vs. automation is involved for the 200 seed PAGs that drive the 10K scenes, which affects scalability claims.

The scene generation experiments are evaluated only via a fairly small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes) and qualitative figures; no quantitative physical-plausibility metrics (e.g., penetration rate, contact accuracy against ground truth, FID-like distributional metrics) are reported for the generation task, limiting the strength of the generative-quality claims.

Comparison in Sec 5.2 is only against InstructScene/3D-FRONT; no comparison to more recent contact-aware or physics-based scene generation baselines (e.g., CommonScenes, RoomCraft, mentioned in related work) is provided, making it hard to judge how much of the improvement is attributable to the PAG representation versus the larger/denser PARSE-10K dataset itself.

The VLM baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0) are evaluated zero-shot/off-the-shelf while the proposed model is fine-tuned directly on PARSE-10K test-distribution-matched data; while a COCO generalization check is mentioned, more extensive analysis of generalization to real-world imagery beyond the synthetic PARSE-10K domain would strengthen claims of broad utility.

The relation vocabulary (Table 4) is a fixed, hand-designed dictionary of part-level relations, which may not generalize to arbitrary novel object categories or long-tail relations not covered by the 132-category asset library and default-surface heuristics.

Some quantitative results (e.g., 97.4% visual relation accuracy) appear very close to ceiling, raising a question of whether the MCQ evaluation protocol (multiple choice with limited distractors) may be relatively easy/saturating rather than a fully rigorous test of spatial reasoning, though this is a presentation/evaluation-design point rather than a fundamental flaw.
